01.r: Puts the statement outside any possible argument.
01.n: Abbott-Smith treats it, as a preposition with the genitive, as 'separate from, apart from, without'.

02.r: Adds a general principle to the argument.

03.r: No dispute of any kind is possible here.

04.n: Abbott-Smith derives it from ἀντιλέγω, literally 'speak against', and gives 'gain-saying, strife'. The BSB folds the whole phrase into one word, 'indisputably'.

05.r: With the adjective it makes a noun: the lesser one.

06.r: The one of lower rank, who receives the blessing.
06.n: The form is neuter, 'the lesser (thing)', which states the rule in general terms rather than naming a person; the DRC's 'that which is less' shows this. Abbott-Smith gives 'less, in age, rank or quality' and cites this verse. In the passage the rule is applied to Abraham, blessed by Melchizedek; that is a reading of the context, as the verse itself states only the rule.

07.r: Marks the one who gives the blessing.

08.r: With the adjective it makes a noun: the better one.

09.r: The one of higher rank, who gives the blessing; in the passage, Melchizedek.
09.n: Abbott-Smith explains that it is properly the comparative of a word for 'strong', but is often used as the comparative of 'good': better. The Geneva and BSB render 'greater'.

10.r: Receives the blessing that the greater gives.
10.n: Present passive: a standing rule, not a single event. Abbott-Smith notes that the Septuagint uses the verb chiefly for Hebrew בָּרַךְ.
